An operator runs OSPF on all the routers in its network. The operator plans to migrate the control plane functions of every router to a remote controller.
After the migration, which operation does each router still perform itself?

options.text: The router runs OSPF with its neighbors to keep its own link-state database current.
The router computes its own forwarding table, and the controller only collects copies of it.
The router asks the controller for the output port of each packet that arrives.
The router looks up each arriving packet in its local forwarding table and forwards it.

why: Forwarding is data plane work, so it stays at the router. Each router looks up each arriving packet in its local table. Computing routes and forwarding tables is control plane work, so it moves to the controller. The routers stop running OSPF. The controller computes the table of each router and installs it there. The router forwards each packet itself. Asking the controller about each packet would add delay to every packet.

stem:
A router performs the following five tasks.
1. The router looks up the destination address of each packet in its forwarding table. 2. The router sends an ICMP error message to the source when the TTL of a packet has run out. 3. The switching fabric carries each packet from its input port to its output port. 4. The router runs OSPF to build its routing table. 5. The output port decides which queued packet goes out on the link next.
Which three tasks add to the delay of every packet that crosses the router?

options.text: Tasks 1, 2 and 3.
Tasks 1, 3 and 5.
Tasks 1, 3 and 4.
Tasks 2, 3 and 5.

why: Tasks 1, 3 and 5 happen for every packet: the lookup, the trip across the fabric, and output scheduling. Each one adds to the delay of every packet. Task 2 happens only for the rare packet whose TTL has run out. Task 4, OSPF, builds the routing table in the background. It does not handle each packet.

stem:
Consider an early router that switches packets via memory. The input ports and output ports work as I/O devices controlled by the routing processor. The memory of the routing processor supports at most B packet reads or packet writes per second.
What limit does the memory place on the forwarding throughput of the router?

options.text: It stays below B/2 packets per second, since each packet is written in and then read out.
It can reach B packets per second, since each packet needs one memory operation to cross.
It can reach 2B packets per second, since one packet's write can overlap another's read.
It stays below B/N packets per second for N ports, since the ports take turns on the memory.

why: Each packet is written into memory and then read out. That is two memory operations per packet. The memory does one operation at a time, so the router moves fewer than B/2 packets per second. A write cannot overlap a read. The number of ports does not change the limit.
caption: Switching via memory

stem:
Consider a router that switches packets via a bus. When an input port receives a packet, the input port adds an internal header that designates the output port. The input port then sends the packet onto the bus. Packets arrive at several input ports at the same time.
What limits the forwarding rate of the router?

options.text: The routing processor, since each packet raises an interrupt and is copied through its memory.
The bus, since it carries one packet at a time and its speed caps the speed of the router.
The output ports, since each output port receives the packet and has to process it.
The internal header, since the designated output port must strip it from every packet.

why: The bus carries one packet at a time, so the speed of the bus limits the router. The routing processor is not on the path. Every output port sees the packet, but only the chosen port keeps it and removes the internal header. That small step does not limit the rate.
caption: Switching via shared bus

stem:
A router uses a crossbar switch to connect N input ports to N output ports. The switching fabric closes a crosspoint to connect an input port to an output port.
How many buses does the crossbar switch need?

options.text: N^2 buses: one bus for each crosspoint, so that each input can reach each output at once.
N buses: each port's bus carries its input traffic in and its output traffic back out.
2N buses: N horizontal input buses and N vertical output buses that meet at crosspoints.
N + 1 buses: one horizontal bus per input, plus one shared bus that the outputs listen to.

why: Each input port has a horizontal bus, and each output port has a vertical bus. That makes 2N buses. They cross at N^2 crosspoints, and a crosspoint is not a bus. N buses are too few, because inputs and outputs need separate buses. No output bus is shared, so the count is not N + 1.

stem:
Consider a router that uses a crossbar switch with input ports A, B and C and output ports X, Y and Z. No other transfers are in progress. Input port A has a packet for output port Z. Input port C has a packet for output port X.
Can the two packets cross the switching fabric at the same time?

options.text: No, because a crossbar carries one packet at a time when several inputs are active.
No, because the A-to-Z path crosses the C-to-X path, and the crossing blocks one of the transfers.
Yes, provided the fabric runs twice as fast as the links, since two packets cross it.
Yes, because the two transfers use different input buses and different output buses.

why: The fabric closes two crosspoints, A to Z and C to X. The two transfers use different buses, so both packets cross at once. Buses that cross do not block each other unless their crosspoint is closed. The fabric does not need to run faster.
caption: Crossbar switch

stem:
Consider a router that uses a crossbar switch with input ports A, B and C and output ports X, Y and Z. Packets wait in input queues and are served first-come first-served. The packet at the head of the input queue of port A is destined for output port Y. The packet at the head of the input queue of port B is also destined for output port Y. Other packets wait behind the head of each input queue.
What happens when both packets try to cross the switching fabric at the same time?

options.text: One transfer goes ahead; the other packet waits in its input queue and blocks packets behind it.
Both go ahead, since the output bus interleaves the bits of the two packets in the same interval.
The fabric sends one packet to a free output port instead, and that port forwards it onward.
The fabric drops one of the two packets, since a crossbar has no place to hold the one that loses.

why: Output Y takes one packet at a time, so one transfer waits. The waiting packet stays at the head of its input queue. The packets behind it wait too, even if their outputs are free. This is head-of-line blocking. The fabric does not mix the bits of two packets, send a packet to another output, or drop the waiting packet.
caption: Crossbar with input queues

stem:
A router uses service differentiation. It gives the traffic sent by different customers different quality-of-service guarantees.
What additional per-packet work does service differentiation require from the router at high speed?

options.text: Sending each packet to the routing processor, which looks up the service guarantee that its customer bought.
Keeping a separate forwarding table for each service guarantee on each line card, and choosing among them.
Classifying each packet by fields other than its destination, such as its source or application.
Looking up each packet's destination a second time, in a table that maps destinations to service guarantees.

why: Service differentiation treats packets differently based on more than their destination. So the router must sort each packet by other header fields, such as its source or its application. This is called packet classification. The routing processor is not asked about each packet. A second destination lookup still sorts packets only by destination. Separate forwarding tables only change the output port, not the service a packet gets.

stem:
Before 1993, IPv4 used classful addressing. A network prefix could be only 8, 16 or 24 bits long. In 1993, CIDR replaced classful addressing.
Why does a router that uses CIDR need longest prefix matching instead of exact matching?

options.text: Each address matches only one prefix, but the router may have to try all 32 lengths to find it.
CIDR made the prefixes shorter, so an exact match on the full 32-bit address now fails.
The address no longer shows the prefix length, and one address can match several prefixes.
Longest prefix matching needs fewer memory accesses per lookup than an exact match does.

why: Under classful addressing, the first bits of an address showed the prefix length, so an exact match worked. With CIDR, a prefix can have any length, and the address does not show it. One address can match several prefixes, such as a large block and a smaller block inside it, and the router picks the longest. Exact matching used only the network part of the address. CIDR allows both shorter and longer prefixes. Longest prefix matching takes more work.

stem:
The forwarding table of a router holds two entries:
10.0.0.0/8, next hop provider P
10.1.2.0/24, next hop provider Q
A packet with destination address 10.1.2.7 arrives at the router.
How does the router handle this packet?

options.text: It forwards the packet to provider P via the 10.0.0.0/8 entry.
It forwards the packet to provider Q via the 10.1.2.0/24 entry.
It drops the packet, since no entry matches the address exactly.
It splits the traffic, sending packets in turn to P and to Q.

why: Both prefixes match 10.1.2.7. The router picks the longer one, the /24, so the packet goes to provider Q. No exact match is needed. The router does not split traffic between the two entries.

stem:
A router reaches the address block 10.0.0.0/8 through provider P. One customer inside that block uses the addresses 10.1.2.0/24. That customer moved to a different provider Q and kept its addresses. The forwarding table of the router now holds two entries:
10.0.0.0/8, next hop provider P
10.1.2.0/24, next hop provider Q
A packet with the destination address 10.1.2.7 arrives at the router. The address 10.1.2.7 falls inside both prefixes. The router forwards the packet to provider Q.
Why does the router use the 10.1.2.0/24 entry rather than the 10.0.0.0/8 entry?

options.text: The /24 entry was added to the table more recently than the /8 entry.
The /24 entry offers a shorter path to 10.1.2.7 than the /8 entry.
The /24 entry has a lower-cost path to 10.1.2.7 than the /8 entry.
The /24 prefix is the longest of the prefixes that match 10.1.2.7.

why: Both prefixes match 10.1.2.7. The router uses the longest matching prefix, the /24. How new an entry is does not matter. The length or cost of a path does not matter either. Those are routing metrics, which the control plane uses to build the table. The lookup compares only prefix lengths.

stem:
A backbone router carries about 250,000 concurrent flows of short duration. The router keeps a cache of recently seen destination addresses.
The cache lets the router skip most lookups in the forwarding table.

options.text: True
False

why: With about 250,000 short flows at once, a recently seen destination is rarely seen again while it is still in the cache. The cache finds few addresses, and most packets still need a full lookup.

stem:
A unibit trie stores a database of IP prefixes. A search reads the destination address one bit at a time, starting at the root.
What is the largest number of child pointers that a node of the trie can hold?

options.text: One pointer, which leads to the next node on the search path.
Two pointers, a 0-pointer and a 1-pointer, one per bit value.
Three pointers: a 0-pointer, a 1-pointer and a prefix pointer.
A number that grows with the count of prefixes below the node.

why: Each node has a 0-pointer and a 1-pointer, one per bit value. Either one may be empty. A stored prefix sits inside the node, not behind a third pointer. The number of prefixes below a node does not change its number of pointers.

stem:
A unibit trie stores a database of IP prefixes. A search for a destination address starts at the root and moves down the trie one node at a time.
At each node, what decides which child pointer the search follows?

options.text: The prefix stored at the node, after the search compares it with the address bits.
The skip count stored at the node, which says how many address bits to jump over.
The side that leads to a longer prefix, after the search looks down both sides.
The next bit of the address: a 0 takes the 0-pointer, and a 1 takes the 1-pointer.

why: The next bit of the address picks the pointer: a 0 takes the 0-pointer, and a 1 takes the 1-pointer. The prefix stored at a node is only remembered as the best match so far. It does not steer the search. A skip count, used in Patricia tries, says how many bits to skip, not which way to go. The search never looks down both sides. It follows one path.

stem:
Consider a unibit trie that stores the prefixes P1 to P9. The prefix P3 = 11001* is 5 bits long. No other prefix in the database begins with the same 4 bits as P3. The trie could store the last 2 bits of P3 as two nodes, each with only one pointer. Instead, the trie stores the last 2 bits of P3 as the text string 01, in the node that holds P9.
Why does the trie store the last 2 bits of P3 as a text string?

options.text: It cuts the search from 32 memory accesses to a few, which fits the lookup budget.
Each bit with no branching would otherwise take a whole node, and that wastes memory.
Without the string, the search could reach P3 by two paths and return the wrong prefix.
The string lets the search skip the 2 bits without comparing them with the address.

why: Without the string, each of the last 2 bits of P3 would need a whole node, with one empty pointer. That wastes memory. The string 01 stores the same 2 bits in less space. The search still compares the 2 bits with the address, and there is still only one path to P3. In a dense trie, compression barely shortens the search, so it does not fix the lookup budget.
caption: Unibit trie: compressed branch P9

stem:
Consider a unibit trie that stores the following five prefixes:
Q1 = 1*
Q2 = 00*
Q3 = 101*
Q4 = 1010*
Q5 = 111*
A packet arrives with a destination address that begins with 10110.
Which prefix does the search return for this address?

options.text: Q1 = 1*, the first prefix the search passed before it found an empty pointer.
Q3 = 101*, the last prefix the search passed before it found an empty pointer.
Q4 = 1010*, the last prefix the search passed before it found an empty pointer.
No prefix, since the search failed before it reached the last bit of the address.

why: The search follows the bits 1, 0 and 1. It passes Q1 and then Q3, and it remembers each one. The fourth bit is 1, but the node that holds Q3 has no 1-pointer. So the search stops and returns Q3, the last prefix it passed. Q3 is longer than Q1. Q4 = 1010* does not match, because the fourth bit of the address is 1.
caption: Unibit trie

stem:
Consider a unibit trie that stores the following five prefixes:
Q1 = 01*
Q2 = 0110*
Q3 = 10*
Q4 = 111*
Q5 = 1101*
The database holds no default route. A packet arrives with a destination address that begins with 11001.
Which prefix does the search return for this address?

options.text: Q5 = 1101*, since it shares the first 3 bits of the address, more than any other prefix.
Q4 = 111*, since the search backs up one node and follows the other pointer instead.
No prefix: the search fails before it passes a stored prefix, so nothing matches.
Q3 = 10*, the last prefix the search passed before it found an empty pointer.

why: The search follows the bits 1, 1 and 0 and passes no stored prefix. The fourth bit is 0, but the node it has reached has only a 1-pointer. So the search stops with no match. Q5 = 1101* does not match, because its fourth bit is 1. The search does not back up to try another pointer. Q3 = 10* does not match, because the second bit of the address is 1.
caption: Unibit trie

stem:
The forwarding table of a backbone router holds about 47,000 prefixes. Two tries are built from this table. The first is a plain binary trie, which uses one node for every bit. The second compresses every one-way branch, a chain of nodes that each have only one child, into a single node.
How does compression affect the average height of the trie, and why?

options.text: It cuts the height by about half, because each compressed node replaces a whole chain of nodes.
It lowers the height only a little, because few nodes along a lookup path have just one child each.
It lowers the height only a little, because backbone prefixes are short, so the trie is already shallow.
It leaves the height unchanged, because compression saves memory but does not shorten any lookup path.

why: Compression removes only chains of nodes with one child. A backbone table is densely populated, so few nodes along a lookup path have just one child. So there are few chains to remove, and the height drops only a little, far from half. The small gain comes from the lack of chains, not from short prefixes: the trie is not shallow. Each chain that is compressed still shortens the paths through it, so the height does drop.

stem:
Consider a unibit trie for the prefix database P1 to P9. A destination address begins with the bits 11001. The search starts at the root of the trie.
Which prefix does the search return?

options.text: P9, because the search passes P4, reaches P9, and the 01 string does not match.
P4, because 1* is the first prefix the search matches, and the first match is returned.
P3, because the search passes P4 and P9, matches the 01 string, and then reaches P3.
P2, because the second bit is 1, and the 11 branch of the trie ends at the prefix 111*.

why: The bits 1, 1 and 0 lead past P4 to the node that holds P9. The string 01 in that node matches the next two bits, so the search reaches P3. The search returns the last prefix it passes, which is the longest match. So it returns P3, not P4 or P9. The branch toward P2 = 111* is left behind at the third bit.
caption: Unibit trie

stem:
A multibit trie uses a stride of 8. Each step of a search reads 8 bits of a 32-bit IPv4 address.
How many entries does each node of the trie hold?

options.text: 8 entries, one for each bit that the node reads.
16 entries, two for each bit that the node reads.
4 entries, one for each 8-bit step in a 32-bit address.
256 entries, one for each value the 8 bits can take.

why: Each node reads the next 8 bits of the address. Those 8 bits can form 2^8 = 256 different patterns, from 00000000 to 11111111. The node holds one entry for each pattern, so it has 256 entries. Some entries may be empty, because no prefix continues through that pattern. So a node always has 256 entries, but it can have fewer than 256 children.

stem:
A multibit trie uses a stride of 8. Each step of a search reads 8 bits of a 32-bit IPv4 address.
What is the worst-case number of memory accesses for a lookup?

options.text: 4, one memory access for each 8-bit step of the address.
5, four steps plus one more access to read the prefix.
8, two per step: one for the pointer and one for the prefix.
32, one memory access for each bit of the address.

why: Each step reads 8 bits of the address in one memory access. A 32-bit address has four groups of 8 bits, so a search takes at most 4 accesses. Each access brings back the pointer and the stored prefix together, so no step needs an extra access.

stem:
Consider a router that stores its forwarding table in a unibit trie and looks up 32-bit IPv4 addresses. A lookup reads the trie one node at a time, and reading one node takes one memory access of 50 nsec. Assume that the router has a budget of 300 nsec for each address lookup, so that it keeps up with packets arriving back to back.
The worst-case lookup finishes within the 300 nsec budget.

options.text: True
False

why: A unibit trie reads one bit at each node, so the worst case visits 32 nodes. That is 32 accesses of 50 nsec each, or 1,600 nsec (more than five times the budget).

stem:
A fixed-stride trie reads k bits of the destination address at each step of a search. The prefix database holds prefixes of many different lengths.
Which prefix lengths can the trie store directly, without changing the prefix?

options.text: Any length up to 32, since a step can stop partway through its k bits.
Only lengths shorter than k, since each fits inside a single step.
Only lengths that are multiples of k, such as k, 2k and 3k bits.
Only the length k itself, the number of bits every node reads.

why: Each step reads exactly k bits, so a search can stop only after k, 2k, 3k bits, and so on. Only prefixes of those lengths fit. A step cannot stop partway. A prefix shorter than k ends inside the first step, so it does not fit either. The trie has several levels, so every multiple of k fits, not only k.

stem:
A fixed-stride trie reads k bits of the destination address at each step of a search. The prefix database holds prefixes of many different lengths. Some of these lengths are not multiples of k.
How is a prefix whose length is not a multiple of k stored in the trie?

options.text: It is padded with 0 bits up to the next multiple of k, which makes one longer prefix.
It is replaced by longer prefixes, at the next multiple of k, that cover the same addresses.
It is cut back to the previous multiple of k, and the bits beyond that point are dropped.
It is kept in a separate table, which is searched when the trie itself finds no match.

why: Controlled prefix expansion replaces the prefix with longer prefixes, whose length is the next multiple of k. The new prefixes are all the ways to extend the original prefix to that length. Each one keeps the same next hop as the original. Together they cover exactly the same addresses as the original prefix. Padding with 0 bits covers only part of those addresses, and cutting back covers extra ones. A separate table would add a second search.

stem:
Consider a fixed-stride trie with a stride of 3. Each step of a search reads 3 bits of the address, so a search can stop only after 3, 6 or 9 bits, and so on. For this reason, every prefix stored in the trie must have a length of 3, 6, 9 and so on. The prefix database holds P3 = 11001*, which is 5 bits long. P3 ends in the middle of a step, so the trie cannot store it as it is.
Which prefixes replace P3 in the trie?

options.text: 110* alone, cut back to the previous multiple of 3.
110010* and 110011*, the two prefixes of length 6.
110010* alone, padding the missing bit with a 0.
110000* to 110111*, the eight prefixes under 110.

why: Adding a 0 or a 1 to P3 gives 110010* and 110011*. Together they cover exactly the addresses of P3. Cutting P3 back to 110* covers too many addresses. Adding only a 0 covers half of them. Expanding from 110 gives eight prefixes, and six of them cover addresses outside P3.
caption: Fixed-stride trie with a stride of 3

stem:
Consider a router that extends every prefix to 6 bits using controlled prefix expansion. Its database holds two prefixes:
P6 = 1000*, next hop A
P7 = 100000*, next hop B
Expanding P6 gives 100000*, 100001*, 100010* and 100011*, all with next hop A. The first of these is the same as P7.
Which next hop does the router use for addresses that begin with 100000?

options.text: Next hop A, because the expansion of P6 replaces the entry that P7 held.
Next hop B, because P7 was longer than P6 before expansion, so it is the longer match.
Both, because the router sends these packets alternately to A and to B.
Neither, because two prefixes that collide cancel out and the entry is left empty.

why: Before expansion, P7 had 6 bits and P6 had only 4. So P7 is the more specific prefix for these addresses, and the longest-match rule picks it. Expansion must not change that, so the router keeps P7 and drops the colliding expansion of P6.
caption: Controlled prefix expansion

stem:
Consider a router that extends every prefix to 4 bits using controlled prefix expansion. Its database holds two prefixes:
P1 = 10*, next hop A
P2 = 101*, next hop B
Expanding P1 gives 1000*, 1001*, 1010* and 1011*, all with next hop A. Expanding P2 gives 1010* and 1011*, both with next hop B.
Which next hop does the router store for 1010* and 1011*?

options.text: Next hop A, because P1 was expanded first and its entries were already in place.
Next hop B, because P2 was longer than P1 before expansion, so it is the longer match.
Next hop A, because P1 covers more addresses, so its expansions take priority.
Neither, because neither prefix was in the table at 4 bits before expansion.

why: Before expansion, P2 had 3 bits and P1 had only 2. So P2 is the more specific prefix for addresses that begin with 101, and the longest-match rule picks it. Expansion must not change that, so the router stores next hop B for 1010* and 1011*. Next hop A stays for 1000* and 1001*.
caption: Controlled prefix expansion

stem:
Consider a fixed-stride trie with a stride of 3 that stores three prefixes: P3 = 11001*, P4 = 1* and P9 = 110*. A destination address begins with 110000.
What does the search return?

options.text: P9, the last stored prefix the search passed before it met the empty entry.
No prefix: the empty entry ends the search with no match; the packet is dropped.
P3, the last stored prefix the search passed before it met the empty entry.
P4, the first stored prefix the search passed before it met the empty entry.

why: The search remembers P9 at the 110 entry of the root. The 000 entry of the child node is empty, so the search stops and returns P9. An empty entry ends the search, but it does not cancel P9. P3 does not match 110000. P4 = 1* also matches, but P9 = 110* is longer.
caption: Fixed-stride trie with a stride of 3

stem:
Consider a fixed-stride trie with a stride of 3. A destination address begins with 100011. At the root node, the search takes the 100 entry, which holds the stored prefix P8 and a pointer to a child node.
What does the search return?

options.text: P8: the root's 100 entry holds P8, and a search returns the first stored prefix it finds.
P6: the child's 011 entry holds P6 and has no pointer, so the search ends there.
P7: the child node holds P7, the longest prefix in that node, so the search returns it.
No prefix: the original database holds no length-6 prefix that begins with 100011.

why: The search remembers P8 and follows the pointer. In the child of 100, the 011 entry holds an expansion of P6 and has no pointer. So the search ends and returns P6, the last prefix it passed, not the first. P7 = 100000* does not match 100011. P6 = 1000* matches, because the address begins with 1000. The prefix does not need to be 6 bits long.
caption: Fixed-stride trie with a stride of 3

stem:
Consider a fixed-stride trie with a stride of 3 that stores the prefixes P1 to P9.
What does the 100 entry of the root node hold, and why?

options.text: P8 and a pointer, because the pointer leads to the child node that holds the expansions of P8.
P8 and a pointer, because P8 ends at this entry and the longer P6 and P7 continue below it.
P8 and a pointer, because the pointer leads to the next hop of P8 and P8 picks the child to visit.
P8 and a pointer, because a search that fails in the child node backs up to the root to read P8.

why: P8 = 100* ends at the root's 100 entry, so the entry stores P8. P8 is already 3 bits long and has no expansions. P6 = 1000* and P7 = 100000* also begin with 100 and are longer. So the entry also needs a pointer to the child node that stores them. A search on 100 remembers P8 as it follows the pointer, and never backs up. It returns P8 only if the child node has no longer match.
caption: Fixed-stride trie with a stride of 3

stem:
Consider a multibit trie with a stride of 2, so each node reads 2 bits of the address. The trie was built from the following five prefixes, after controlled prefix expansion to lengths 2 and 4:
Q11 = 1*
Q12 = 10*
Q13 = 1011*
Q14 = 110*
Q15 = 1111*
A packet arrives with a destination address that begins with 1110.
Which prefix does the search return for this address?

options.text: Q11 = 1*, the last prefix the search passed, stored in the 11 entry of the root.
Q15 = 1111*, the last prefix the search passed, stored in the 11 entry of the child.
No prefix: the 10 entry of the child node is empty, so the search finds no match.
Q14 = 110*, the last prefix the search passed, stored in the child node below 11.

why: At the root, the first 2 bits are 11. The 11 entry holds Q11, expanded from 1* to 11*, and a pointer. The search remembers Q11 and follows the pointer. In the child node, the 10 entry is empty. So the search stops and returns Q11, the prefix it remembered at the root. Q15 = 1111* does not match, because bits 3 and 4 are 10. Q14 = 110* expands to 1100* and 1101*, and neither matches.
caption: Multibit trie with a stride of 2

stem:
A variable-stride trie lets each node read a different number of bits. A dynamic program chooses these strides. It builds a unibit trie of the database, then works up from the bottom, reusing the best strides found for each subtrie. It runs about once a day.
The dynamic program chooses the strides to minimize the memory that the trie uses.

options.text: True
False

why: The line rate and the memory speed fix the number of memory accesses first, which fixes the height of the trie. For that height, the dynamic program picks the strides that use the least memory.

stem:
Consider edge router R, which connects three subnets to two outbound links, L1 and L2. Site S1 is in Subnet 1, site S2 is in Subnet 2, and the third subnet is Subnet X. Links L1 and L2 lead to remote networks, including Subnet D, which holds host D, and Subnet Y.
Router R forwards traffic by longest prefix matching on the destination IP address. Router R must also apply three rules:
Rule 1: send video traffic from site S1 to host D over link L1, and all other traffic to D over link L2.
Rule 2: drop all traffic from site S2.
Rule 3: reserve 50 Mbps for traffic from Subnet X to Subnet Y.
Which of the three rules can router R apply using longest prefix matching on the destination IP address alone?

options.text: Rule 2 only. A table entry for Subnet 2 matches the packets that site S2 sends.
Rules 1 and 3 only. An entry for Subnet D or Subnet Y selects the traffic each rule covers.
All three. The operator can add a more specific destination prefix to match each rule.
None. The lookup returns the next hop per prefix, regardless of the source or traffic type.

why: Longest prefix matching reads only the destination address. Every packet to one prefix gets the same next hop, however specific the prefix is. Each rule also depends on the source, and Rule 1 depends on the traffic type as well. An entry for Subnet 2 matches packets sent to Subnet 2, not packets sent from site S2. Matching several header fields at once is packet classification.
caption: Edge router R between source and destination subnets

stem:
Consider a router that classifies packets by a linear search through a large list of rules. In front of the search, the router keeps a cache of recent results. On a cache hit, the router finds the result in one memory access. On a cache miss, the router runs the full linear search, which takes thousands of times longer than a cache hit. The cache hit rate is 98 percent.
Most of the average classification time comes from the cache misses.

options.text: True
False

why: A cache miss still costs a full linear search. Only 2 percent of packets miss, but each miss takes thousands of times as long as a hit. The misses add far more to the average than the hits do. A high hit rate cannot hide a slow miss.
caption: A classification cache in front of a linear search

stem:
Consider a two-field packet classifier that matches packets on a destination prefix and a source prefix. The classifier is a set-pruning trie. A destination trie indexes the destination prefixes, and each valid destination node points to its own source trie.
Let D be one valid destination node, such as 00*.
Which rules must the source trie at node D hold?

options.text: Only the rules whose destination prefix is exactly D, stored once in that source trie.
Every rule whose destination prefix is D or a longer prefix below D, such as 000* or 001*.
Every rule whose destination prefix is D or a shorter prefix above D, such as *.
Only the rules that remain after broader rules overlapping with D's rules are pruned out.

why: A packet that matches destination prefix D also matches every shorter prefix of D, up to the wildcard *. Rules with those destinations can apply to it, so the source trie at D holds copies of them all. One walk down that trie finds the least-cost rule. Keeping only the rules for D is the backtracking layout. A longer prefix such as 000* need not match the packet.
caption: A set-pruning trie: a destination trie with source tries

stem:
Consider a router that performs two-field packet classification on N rules with a set-pruning trie. Some rules have the wildcard destination prefix *.
As N grows, which cost of the set-pruning trie grows fastest in the worst case?

options.text: Lookup time, because each search climbs back up to check the source tries of ancestors.
Update time, because the switch pointers must be recomputed every time a rule changes.
Power use, because the router compares every stored rule in parallel on each lookup.
Memory, because rules with broad destination prefixes are copied into many source tries.

why: A rule with the wildcard destination * matches every destination. Set pruning copies such a rule into the source trie of every destination prefix, so memory can grow to about N squared. A lookup is still one walk down the destination trie and one source trie. Climbing to ancestor tries is the cost of backtracking, and recomputing switch pointers is the cost of the grid of tries. Comparing every rule in parallel is how a ternary CAM works.

stem:
Consider a router that classifies packets on two fields, the destination prefix and the source prefix. The rule database of the router contains the six rules in the table. The router stores these rules in a set-pruning trie. Each distinct destination prefix in the table has its own source trie.
In how many source tries does the set-pruning trie store rule R3?

options.text: One: only the source trie at its own destination prefix, *.
Four: the source tries of the other destination prefixes in the table.
Five: the source tries of all the destination prefixes in the table.
Six: one source trie for each of the six rules in the table.

why: The destination prefix * matches every destination, so rule R3 can apply to any packet. Set pruning copies R3 into the source trie of every destination prefix in the table: *, 1*, 10*, 11* and 101*. That makes five tries. The trie at * counts, because a packet whose destination starts with 0 ends its destination search there. R2 and R6 share 10*, so six rules give five tries. Keeping R3 only at * is the backtracking layout.
caption: A rule database with six two-field rules

stem:
Consider a router that performs two-field packet classification on destination and source prefixes. The router holds N rules, and each field is at most W bits long. The router replaces its set-pruning trie with a backtracking trie.
What does the router give up?

options.text: Lookup speed.
Accuracy.
Update speed.
Memory.

why: Backtracking stores each rule once, in the source trie of its own destination prefix. Memory falls from O(N squared) to O(NW). A matching rule may sit at an ancestor destination prefix, so the search climbs back up and checks up to W source tries. Worst-case lookup rises to O(W squared). No rule is missed. Switch pointers belong to the grid of tries.

stem:
Consider a router that classifies packets on two header fields: the destination prefix and the source prefix. Each field is 32 bits long. The classifier is designed as a backtracking trie built from 1-bit tries.
In the worst case, about how many memory accesses does it take to classify a single packet?

options.text: 64 accesses, 32 in the destination trie plus 32 in a single source trie.
32 accesses, one for each of the 32 header bits in a single walk.
1,024 accesses, because up to 32 source tries are searched at 32 each.
8 accesses, one for each 4-bit step through a 32-bit field.

why: W is the number of bits in each field, so W = 32 here. With 1-bit tries, one walk down a trie takes up to W accesses. Backtracking walks the destination trie, then searches the source trie of the longest match and of every ancestor with a nonempty source trie. In the worst case, that is W source tries at W accesses each, or 32 × 32 = 1,024. A count of 32 is a single walk, and 64 is two walks. A count of 8 is a single walk with 4-bit tries.
caption: Two 32-bit header fields and a 1-bit trie

stem:
Consider a router that classifies packets on two header fields. The router replaces its backtracking trie with a grid of tries.
The grid of tries stores a precomputed switch pointer at each failure point in the source tries.
What does the router give up, compared with backtracking?

options.text: Memory.
Update speed.
Accuracy.
Worst-case lookup speed.

why: Switch pointers are computed from the rule set, so a rule change means recomputing them. Updates are far rarer than lookups, so the trade is acceptable. Each rule is still stored once, so memory stays O(NW). The pointers replace the climb back up the destination trie, so the worst-case lookup falls to O(W). The tries they skip hold only source prefixes shorter than the best match already found.
caption: A grid of tries with switch pointers

stem:
Consider a grid of tries for two-field packet classification. Each rule is stored exactly once in the source trie of its own destination prefix node. At every failure point in a source trie, the structure embeds a precomputed switch pointer.
Which step of the backtracking search do the switch pointers replace?

options.text: Traversing the source trie associated with the longest matching destination prefix.
Tracking and updating the best matching rule found so far during the search.
Climbing back up the destination trie to search the source tries of ancestor nodes.
Re-running the destination prefix lookup, because the pointer caches its earlier result.

why: When a source trie search fails, plain backtracking climbs back up the destination trie to search the source tries of ancestors. A precomputed switch pointer at the failure point jumps straight to the next source trie that could still hold a match. The search still walks the source trie at the longest destination match, and it still tracks the best match so far. The destination lookup runs once.
caption: A grid of tries with a switch pointer

topic: Scheduling and Head of Line Blocking
stem:
Consider an input-queued crossbar switch where each input port maintains a single FIFO queue. The crossbar is scheduled using the take a ticket scheme.
During the current packet time slot:
The head-of-line packet at Input A is destined for Output 1.
The head-of-line packet at Input B is also destined for Output 1.
The scheduler awards Output 1 to Input A.
The second packet in queue at Input B is destined for Output 2, which is idle.
What packet does Input B transmit during this time slot?

options.text: Nothing, because its packet for Output 2 waits behind the head-of-line packet for Output 1.
Its second packet (destined for Output 2), which bypasses the blocked head-of-line packet.
Its head-of-line packet, which Output 1 carries at the same time as Input A's packet.
Its head-of-line packet, redirected to idle Output 2 so that Output 2 does not sit idle.

why: Input B has a single FIFO queue, so only its head-of-line packet can be considered. Output 1 is granted to Input A, so that packet waits. The packet for Output 2 waits behind it, although Output 2 is idle. This wait is head-of-line blocking. A crossbar output connects to one input at a time, and a packet goes only to the output its lookup chose.
caption: An input-queued crossbar with one FIFO queue per input

topic: Scheduling and Head of Line Blocking
stem:
Consider router R, which has an N by N input-queued crossbar switch. The switch is scheduled by the take a ticket algorithm. Each input port uses a single FIFO queue.
Every input queue holds a large number B of packets for Output 1, then B packets for Output 2, and so on up to Output N.
While the switch works through the packets for Output 1, several inputs can send packets at the same time.

options.text: True
False

why: While the switch works through the packets for Output 1, every input has a packet for Output 1 at the head of its queue. Output 1 can take only one packet per time slot, so only one input sends and the other N-1 wait. The other N-1 outputs sit idle. For large B, throughput falls to 1/N of capacity.
caption: The FIFO input queues of a crossbar router

stem:
Consider an N by N crossbar switch with input queueing. The designer replaces the single FIFO queue at each input port with N Virtual Output Queues (VOQs), one per output port.
Why does this change remove head-of-line blocking?

options.text: Each input port can now transmit packets from all N of its VOQs in a single time slot.
Packets for an idle output port no longer share a queue with packets for a busy output port.
Packets for busy output ports are dropped from their VOQs, so they no longer block others.
Concentrator hardware randomly selects winning packets whenever inputs contend for an output.

why: A single FIFO queue causes head-of-line blocking because packets for different outputs share one line. VOQs split the packets at each input port into N queues, one per output. A packet for an idle output can then be scheduled while a packet for a busy output waits in its own VOQ. Each input still sends from one VOQ per time slot. Concentrators belong to Knockout, which removes input queueing instead of splitting it.
caption: A FIFO input queue and virtual output queues

stem:
Consider an input-queued crossbar switch using Virtual Output Queues (VOQs), scheduled by Parallel Iterative Matching (PIM).
In the Request phase of a round, Inputs A, B and C all send requests to Output 3.
How does Output 3 respond in the Grant phase?

options.text: It randomly selects one input among A, B, and C, and grants only that input.
It queues all three requests and grants them in arrival order over later rounds.
It grants the input that sent the fewest requests, to maximize the total matches.
It grants requests to all three inputs at once, letting the inputs decide which one sends.

why: PIM runs three phases in each round: Request, Grant and Accept. In the Grant phase, an output that receives requests from several inputs picks exactly one input at random and grants that input. The choice is random, so it does not depend on arrival order or on how many requests each input sent. The inputs choose among their grants only in the Accept phase.
caption: Inputs A, B and C each request Output 3

stem:
Consider a crossbar switch with Virtual Output Queues (VOQs) and scheduled by Parallel Iterative Matching (PIM).
In the Request phase of the current cell time slot, Input A requests Output 1 and Output 4, and Input B requests Output 1 only. No other input requests Output 4. In the Grant phase, Output 1 picks Input B at random and grants it.
What happens to Input A in the rest of this cell time slot?

options.text: Input A transmits nothing during this cell time slot and retries Output 1 in the next slot.
Output 4 grants Input A, so Input A accepts it and sends to Output 4 in this cell time slot.
Input A transmits to Output 1 immediately after Input B finishes, within the same cell time slot.
Output 4 waits for Output 1 to decide, so Input A receives its grant in the next cell time slot.

why: In PIM, each input requests every output it has queued packets for, and each output grants on its own. Output 4 has only Input A's request, so it grants Input A. Input A holds one grant and accepts it. Input A sends to Output 4 while Input B sends to Output 1. An output connects to one input per cell time slot, so Input A cannot follow Input B on Output 1.
caption: PIM requests and a grant in one cell time slot

stem:
Consider an input-queued crossbar switch using Virtual Output Queues (VOQs) and scheduled by Parallel Iterative Matching (PIM).
Input A holds packets in its VOQs for busy Output 1 and for idle Output 2.
In the Request phase of the current round, Input A requests Output 2 without waiting for its packet for Output 1 to be sent.

options.text: True
False

why: Virtual output queues keep a separate queue for each output port. In the Request phase of PIM, an input sends requests in parallel to all output ports for which it has queued packets. Input A requests Output 1 and Output 2 at the same time.
caption: Virtual output queues (VOQs) at Input A of a crossbar

stem:
Consider an output link queue on router R. The queue is served First-In, First-Out (FIFO) and uses tail drop: when the buffer is full, each newly arriving packet is dropped.
A bulk backup transfer and several interactive remote login sessions share the output link. Traffic rises until the buffer is full.
What is the drawback of FIFO with tail drop in this situation?

options.text: Tail drop discards every packet that reaches the full buffer, so the backup locks out the sessions.
Tail drop selectively discards bulk backup packets first, so the backup flow gets less than its fair share.
Scheduling overhead is too high for gigabit links, so packets wait while the scheduler decides.
Tail drop reorders packets within individual flows, which TCP then reads as congestion signals.

why: Tail drop discards any packet that arrives while the buffer is full, from any flow. The bulk transfer fills the whole buffer. Packets from the remote login sessions then arrive at a full buffer and are dropped. The interactive sessions are locked out. FIFO decisions are fast enough for links above 40 gigabit, and one FIFO queue keeps each flow's packets in order.
caption: A FIFO output queue with tail drop at a router

stem:
Consider an output link queue on router R. The queue is served First-In, First-Out (FIFO) and uses tail drop: when the buffer is full, each newly arriving packet is dropped.
A bulk backup transfer and several remote login sessions share the output link. The backup keeps the buffer full, so packets from the remote login sessions are dropped as they arrive.
What does router R need so that the backup can no longer lock out the remote login sessions?

options.text: A larger buffer, so that remote login packets find free space when they arrive.
A faster FIFO scheduler, so that packets leave before the buffer can fill.
A single queue at the input port instead, so packets wait before they cross the switch.
A way to tell the flows apart, so it can give each flow a fair share of the link.

why: A single FIFO queue with tail drop has no say in which packets it drops, so the backup takes whatever buffer there is. A larger buffer fills the same way. FIFO is already fast enough for links above 40 gigabit, so speed is not the problem. One queue at the input is still one shared queue, and the lockout stays. The router must recognize each flow from its header fields, which is packet classification, so that a scheduler can give each flow its share.
caption: A FIFO output queue with tail drop at a router

stem:
Consider a packet stream that travels a fixed route from a source to a destination. The stream carries one voice call and one file transfer, which can be told apart by their header fields:
Voice call: needs strict low-latency guarantees at every router.
File transfer: needs high throughput, with no strict delay bounds.
How many flows is the packet stream considered to contain?

options.text: One flow, because all of its packets travel the same route from source to destination.
One flow, because all of its packets can be identified from the same header fields.
Two flows, because the two traffic types need different grades of service.
Two flows, because voice packets are smaller than file transfer packets.

why: A flow shares one route and one grade of service. Voice needs strict delay bounds and file transfer does not, so there are two flows. A shared route or shared header fields is not enough. Packet size plays no part.
caption: A stream of voice and file transfer packets

stem:
Consider two flows, F1 and F2, that share a link under plain round robin. Both flows always have packets queued. F1 sends 1,500-byte packets, and F2 sends 100-byte packets.
The router then switches to Deficit Round Robin (DRR), which gives each flow a quantum and a deficit counter.
Which fairness problem of plain round robin does DRR correct?

options.text: Plain round robin grants F2 15 times more bandwidth, because smaller packets finish sooner.
Plain round robin gives no delay bound, which DRR then guarantees with its deficit counter.
Plain round robin gives both flows equal bandwidth, although F1's packets are 15 times larger.
Plain round robin grants F1 15 times more bandwidth, as it counts packets rather than bits.

why: Plain round robin sends one packet per flow in each round. F1's packets are 15 times larger than F2's, so F1 gets 15 times more bandwidth than F2. DRR corrects this by giving each flow a quantum in bytes and tracking its deficit across rounds. DRR guarantees bandwidth and gives no delay guarantee.
caption: Flows F1 and F2 under plain round robin

stem:
Consider an output port scheduled by Deficit Round Robin (DRR). Flow F1 has a quantum Q1 = 600 bytes, and its deficit counter D1 starts at 0.
F1's queue holds three packets, in order: 250 bytes, 700 bytes and 40 bytes.
What does the scheduler do when it visits F1 in this round?

options.text: F1 transmits the 250-byte packet and retains a deficit counter of D1 = 350 bytes for its next turn.
F1 transmits the 250-byte packet, and its deficit counter of 350 bytes is reset to 0 at the end of the turn.
F1 transmits both the 250-byte and 700-byte packets, leaving its deficit counter at -350 bytes.
F1 transmits the 250-byte and 40-byte packets by skipping the 700-byte packet, keeping a deficit of 310 bytes.

why: The scheduler adds Q1 to D1, so F1 has 0 + 600 = 600 bytes of credit. F1 sends the 250-byte head packet, leaving 600 - 250 = 350 bytes. The 700-byte second packet exceeds 350 bytes, so F1's turn ends. F1's queue is not empty, so D1 = 350 carries over to the next round. The deficit counter never goes below zero. DRR also never serves packets out of queue order.
caption: The queue of flow F1 under deficit round robin (DRR)

stem:
Consider a sender whose traffic is covered by a Service Level Agreement (SLA). The SLA sets an agreed traffic rate. The sender bursts above this rate. An edge router can enforce the SLA by traffic policing or by traffic shaping.
How does traffic policing differ from traffic shaping?

options.text: Policing queues non-conforming packets until they conform; shaping drops or marks them at once.
Policing drops or marks non-conforming packets at once; shaping queues them until they conform.
Policing checks the average rate once per second; shaping checks each packet as it arrives.
Policing enforces the long-run average rate; shaping limits the largest burst size.

why: Policing checks each packet against the SLA rate and drops or marks non-conforming packets immediately. Shaping holds excess packets in per-flow queues and releases them at a conforming rate. Both enforce the same agreement; they differ in what happens to the excess.

stem:
Consider a router that polices a flow with a token bucket. Tokens arrive at 1 token per second, and the bucket holds at most 50 tokens. Each packet needs one token.
The flow has been idle, so the bucket is full. Then a burst of 80 packets arrives within 10 milliseconds, too fast for any new token to arrive.
How does the policer handle the 80 packets?

options.text: It passes all 80 packets immediately, and the token count drops to -30.
It passes 1 packet per second, the token rate, and drops or marks the remaining 79 packets.
It passes the first 50 packets immediately, and drops or marks the remaining 30 packets.
It passes the first 50 packets immediately, and buffers the remaining 30 until new tokens arrive.

why: The full bucket holds 50 tokens, so the first 50 packets each take a token and pass immediately. No new tokens arrive during the 10 ms burst, and the token count never goes below zero. The remaining 30 packets find the bucket empty. A policer drops or marks them immediately and does not buffer them. The saved tokens let a quiet flow send a burst above the token rate.
caption: A token bucket policer and a burst

stem:
Consider a router that polices flows F1 and F2, each with its own token bucket. Both buckets receive r = 100 tokens per second. F1's bucket holds at most b = 10 tokens, and F2's holds at most b = 100. Each packet needs one token.
Both flows have been idle, so both buckets are full.
How do the traffic agreements for F1 and F2 differ?

options.text: F2 may keep a higher long-run average, while both flows are held to the same largest burst.
F2 may send a larger burst at once, while both are held to the same long-run average.
F2 may hold up to 100 excess packets in its bucket until they conform, and F1 only 10.
F2 may send a larger burst, and its larger bucket also refills with tokens at a faster rate.

why: The token rate r sets the long-run average, 100 packets per second for both flows. The bucket size b sets the largest burst after an idle period: 10 packets for F1 and 100 for F2. A token bucket holds tokens, not packets, so a policer drops or marks excess packets instead of queuing them. Both buckets gain tokens at the same rate, so F2 does not refill faster.
caption: The token buckets of flows F1 and F2

stem:
Consider an ISP that polices the traffic of customer network C with a token bucket at edge router R. Each packet needs one token.
The Service Level Agreement (SLA) allows an average of 1,000 packets per second over the long run, and a burst of up to 200 packets arriving at once after an idle period. The access link carries at most 10,000 packets per second.
Which token bucket settings enforce this SLA?

options.text: r = 200 tokens per second, b = 1,000 tokens
r = 10,000 tokens per second, b = 200 tokens
r = 1,000 tokens per second, b = 1,000 tokens
r = 1,000 tokens per second, b = 200 tokens

why: The token rate sets the long-run average, so r = 1,000 tokens per second. The bucket size sets the largest burst, so b = 200 tokens. Swapping them allows an average of 200 and bursts of 1,000. A rate of 10,000 matches the link, so it enforces no average. A bucket of 1,000 allows bursts of 1,000, not 200.

stem:
Consider a router that shapes a flow with a leaky bucket. The bucket has a fixed-size buffer and drains at a constant rate r.
A long burst arrives much faster than r and fills the buffer.
What happens to packets that arrive while the buffer is full?

options.text: They are marked as excess traffic and forwarded immediately.
They wait outside the buffer in an overflow queue, preventing packet loss.
They are transmitted immediately at the burst rate because the bucket is full.
They are dropped, while the bucket keeps sending its queued packets at rate r.

why: A leaky bucket shaper buffers arriving packets and leaks them out at a constant rate r. If traffic above r fills the buffer, further packets that arrive at the full bucket are dropped. The bucket is the only buffer, and it never sends faster than r. Marking and forwarding excess packets is what a token bucket policer does.

stem:
Consider a router that shapes a flow with a leaky bucket that drains at rate r. The flow starts sending faster than r, but the bucket still has room.
The router drops the packets that exceed rate r as soon as they arrive.

options.text: True
False

why: Unlike a policer, a leaky bucket shaper does not drop packets arriving above rate r while buffer space remains. The shaper queues them and releases them at rate r. The shaper drops packets only when the buffer is full.
caption: A leaky bucket with room left

stem:
Consider a sender S transmitting bursty traffic to router R, which shapes traffic using a leaky bucket shaper that drains at rate r.
The long-run average transmission rate from sender S is less than r, and the leaky bucket buffer is large enough that it never overflows.
What traffic profile leaves router R?

options.text: The bursts pass through unchanged as they arrive, because the average rate is below r.
The bursts leave intact, each burst delayed as a whole until the bucket has drained.
A smoothed stream no faster than r, with burst packets held in the bucket, sent later.
A smoothed stream no faster than r, with every packet that arrives above rate r dropped.

why: A leaky bucket shaper removes bursts. The shaper buffers burst arrivals and releases them at a steady rate no greater than r. The buffer never overflows, so no packets are dropped.
caption: Bursty traffic into a leaky bucket

stem:
Consider a sender S that sends bursty traffic to router R. Every 2 seconds, a burst of 80 packets arrives within 1 millisecond.
Router R shapes this traffic with a leaky bucket that holds at most 50 packets and leaks 100 packets per second, one every 10 ms. The bucket is empty when the first burst arrives. Each burst is so short that no packet leaves the bucket while it arrives.
The operator of router R wants the bucket to drop no packets. Does this leaky bucket meet that goal?

options.text: No. The 50-packet bucket overflows during each burst, so 30 packets of each burst are dropped.
Yes. The average rate of 40 packets per second is well below the leak rate of 100 packets per second.
Yes. Excess packets above the leak rate wait in the bucket, so no packets are lost.
No. The leaky bucket releases the entire burst at once, exceeding the physical link capacity.

why: The 80-packet burst arrives in 1 ms, and no packet leaves during the burst. The first 50 packets fill the bucket, and the other 30 are dropped. The bucket drains in 0.5 seconds, so every burst meets an empty bucket and loses 30 packets. An average below the leak rate prevents loss only when the bucket holds a whole burst. The bucket sends at its leak rate, so no burst leaves at once.
caption: Sender S and the leaky bucket at router R
